headline: RBA rate hike next week now near-certain as Iran tensions, oil spike and a weak Aussie dollar weigh on markets — Pilbara Minerals had a rough day, down 5.7%.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS had a rough session today, dropping nearly 6%. Lithium sentiment remains weak — there's no big near-term catalyst to push prices higher, and the broader ASX sold off. The long-term EV battery demand story is still intact, but short-term pain continues for lithium miners.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google fell sharply last night, down 3.6% on NASDAQ. No single blowup — but investors are jittery as the AI race heats up, with Gemini 4 expected earlier than planned while rivals OpenAI (GPT-6) and Anthropic are launching cheaper models. Markets may be questioning whether Google can keep pace with the competitive pressure.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two dipped 1.7% last night. The GTA 6 hype continues to build — Rockstar is teasing a reveal — but the market is taking a breather after prior gains. A 97% shareholder vote backing CEO Strauss Zelnick shows strong confidence in the direction; this looks like noise rather than signal.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG slipped 0.6% today alongside the broader ASX, which fell 0.7%. Nothing specific to VDHG — it tracks a diversified global portfolio, so it moved with the market tide. Normal day-to-day volatility.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI edged down 0.5% today. Google (a key holding in most AI ETFs) had a rough night in the US last night, dragging sentiment. Long-term AI investment tailwinds remain strong — multiple motley fool-style outlets named GXAI as a top ASX ETF pick for 2027.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE dipped 0.4% today. Emerging markets broadly tracked the global risk-off tone, with the AUD also weaker. Nothing fundamental has changed with this holding.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS fell only 0.25% today despite a softer night on Wall Street last night. As an ASX-listed ETF tracking the full US market, it absorbed some of that US weakness but held up reasonably well. Still in the green overall — up 3.9% on your investment.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft was the standout last night, edging up 0.5% to close above $500 USD. While Google slid on AI competition fears, MSFT continues to benefit from its deep OpenAI partnership and strong cloud growth narrative. The market is favouring Microsoft's AI story right now.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike next week — almost certain now
watch_today.detail: Multiple sources today confirmed a Reserve Bank rate hike next week is all but locked in. This means your mortgage (if you have one) costs more, and the housing market faces more pressure. For your portfolio, higher rates can weigh on growth stocks and ETFs in the short term — but for a long-term holder, sit tight. This has been well-telegraphed and is mostly priced in.

watch_today.title: Pilbara Minerals (PLS.AX) — another nasty drop today
watch_today.detail: PLS fell 5.7% today to $3.94, deepening an already painful position (you're down 41.5% overall). The lithium market remains soft and there's no near-term catalyst on the horizon. However, the long-term EV battery demand story hasn't broken — this is a high-risk, high-conviction play. No reason to panic-sell into weakness if you believe in the thesis. Hold and watch.

watch_today.title: Google (GOOG) — sharp fall last night, AI race intensifying
watch_today.detail: GOOG dropped 3.6% last night to $334.98 USD. The AI arms race is accelerating — OpenAI just launched GPT-6 (Sol and Luna), Anthropic is cutting prices, and Google's Gemini 4 is being rushed out earlier than planned. Competition is real, but Google still has enormous resources and a strong moat. You're still up 8.9% overall. This is noise for a long-term holder — hold.

watch_today.title: Microsoft (MSFT) — quietly hitting $500, looking strong
watch_today.detail: MSFT nudged above $500 USD last night, up 0.5%, while the rest of NASDAQ sold off. Its deep partnership with OpenAI continues to be a differentiator and markets are rewarding it. You're up 13% on your position. Nothing to do here — the long-term case is intact.

watch_today.title: Oil spiking — watch for inflation ripple effects
watch_today.detail: Crude oil jumped 2% last night to $94 USD a barrel, driven by Iran war tensions. Higher oil means higher petrol prices and can reignite inflation — which could give the RBA more reason to keep rates higher for longer. Watch this space, especially as it affects the cost of living and rate expectations.

watch_today.title: AUD weakening — affects your US holdings' value in AUD
watch_today.detail: The Aussie dollar fell 1.2% last night to 70.3 US cents. A weaker AUD actually boosts the AUD value of your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) — so that's a small silver lining on a rough night. If the RBA hikes next week, the AUD could stabilise or recover slightly.

world.summary: Iran tensions dominated the UN General Assembly this week, with the Iranian president defiantly vowing to fight 'until our last breath' while the US weighs military options. Meanwhile, international bodies are sounding alarms on rising global debt, oil is spiking, and a possible new war is brewing in Africa.

stories.title: Iran's President Defiant at UN: 'We'll Fight Until Our Last Breath'
stories.why_it_matters: Iran's president addressed the UN General Assembly defiantly, declaring Iran will 'fight until our last breath' as conflict with the US escalates. US Secretary of State Rubio says dialogue is on the table but military options remain live. The Iranian president arrived in New York for the UN meeting even as Trump publicly weighed whether to strike a deal or push Iran 'into hell'. This is one of the most serious flashpoints in global geopolitics right now — and it's already pushing oil prices higher, which hits Australians at the petrol pump.

stories.title: Oil Spikes 2% as Iran War Fears Grip Energy Markets
stories.why_it_matters: Crude oil jumped 2% to $94 a barrel last night as the Iran conflict rattles global energy supply. The OECD noted that the AI boom may help cushion the economic blow of a Middle East energy shock — but warned the effect won't last if the conflict drags on. For Australians, this translates directly to higher petrol prices and stickier inflation, which makes the RBA's job harder and rate cuts less likely.

stories.title: A Disastrous New War Threatens in Africa
stories.why_it_matters: The Economist is warning this week that a new, potentially catastrophic war is brewing in Africa — details on the specific region are limited from the article title alone, but The Economist rarely uses the word 'disastrous' lightly. Conflicts in Africa have a track record of destabilising commodity markets, triggering refugee crises, and drawing in outside powers. One to watch as more reporting emerges.

stories.title: Global Debt Warning: Three International Bodies Sound the Alarm
stories.why_it_matters: The IMF, World Bank, and OECD jointly warned this week that soaring government debt and borrowing in major economies poses a serious risk to global financial stability. When the world's biggest economies borrow too much, it can push up interest rates globally, crowd out private investment, and leave governments with less room to respond to future crises. For everyday Australians, it reinforces why interest rates may stay higher for longer worldwide — not just here.

stories.title: OECD: Global Economy Stronger Than Expected, But Threats Mount
stories.why_it_matters: The OECD's latest economic outlook says global growth is holding up better than feared, but risks are mounting — particularly from the Iran conflict, energy prices, and high debt levels. Turkey's growth forecast has been slashed to its lowest since 2020 due to Iran war spillover. The OECD also flagged that AI investment is providing a short-term economic buffer, particularly in tech-heavy economies. The bottom line: the world economy is resilient but walking a tightrope.

markets.summary: A broadly red session all round. The ASX 200 fell 0.7% today while Wall Street last night also slipped — S&P 500 down 0.76%, NASDAQ down 0.69%. Oil jumped 2% on Iran tensions, gold dipped slightly, and the AUD fell over 1% against the USD to 70.3 cents. Not a dramatic sell-off, but the mood is cautious as rate hikes loom and geopolitical risks mount.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Down 0.7% today. Broad-based weakness across the index as rate hike fears and global risk-off sentiment weighed on sentiment.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Fell 0.76% last night. Iran tensions and a spike in oil prices made investors cautious heading into the weekend.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Down 0.69% last night. Google's sharp fall dragged the index, partly offset by Microsoft's small gain.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Jumped 2% last night to $94/barrel — highest in recent weeks — as Iran war fears threatened Middle East supply routes.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold slipped slightly last night. Unusual given the geopolitical tension — suggests some investors are selling gold to cover losses elsewhere.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar fell over 1% to 70.3 US cents last night. Weaker sentiment around Australia + looming rate hike uncertainty are weighing on the currency.

politics.summary: The RBA rate hike drumbeat is getting louder — markets now see a hike next week as near-certain. Treasurer Chalmers is also under the spotlight for a multibillion-dollar blowout in debt costs. Meanwhile, Australia's proposed social media algorithm laws are drawing criticism from the US, and PM Albanese is reviving the misinformation policing debate.

stories.title: RBA Rate Hike Next Week: All But Certain, Worse Could Follow
stories.why_it_matters: Economists and markets now believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates at next Tuesday's meeting — and it might not stop there. Inflation data and a still-tight jobs market are giving the RBA little room to hold. For anyone with a variable-rate mortgage, another hike means another increase in monthly repayments. The housing market is also under pressure, with Reuters reporting Australia's housing sector has 'run out of rescuers' as rate hikes accumulate.

stories.title: Chalmers Reveals Multibillion-Dollar Blowout in Australia's Debt Bill
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has revealed the government's debt interest bill is running significantly higher than expected — a multibillion-dollar blowout. Higher global interest rates mean the government is paying more to service its debt, squeezing the budget. This makes big new spending commitments harder to justify and puts pressure on Labor's economic credentials heading toward the next election cycle.

stories.title: US Calls Australia's Algorithm Opt-Out Laws 'Censorship'
stories.why_it_matters: The US government has criticised Australia's proposed laws that would let people opt out of social media algorithm-driven content feeds, labelling it 'censorship'. Australia is pushing back on Big Tech's control over what users see online — a popular idea with many Australians frustrated with social media rabbit holes. But Washington's criticism adds diplomatic pressure and could complicate trade or tech policy relations between the two countries.

stories.title: Albanese Revives 'Misinformation' Policing Plans
stories.why_it_matters: PM Albanese has quietly put misinformation regulation back on the agenda, with a speech that wasn't publicly released raising questions about what the government is planning. Previous attempts to legislate against online misinformation were shelved after fierce backlash over free speech concerns. Reviving this debate ahead of a federal election cycle is politically risky — it's likely to energise critics who see it as government overreach into what Australians can say and share online.

ai.summary: A massive week in AI. OpenAI dropped its biggest model yet — GPT-6 in two variants — while Google is rushing Gemini 4 to market earlier than planned to keep up. The CEOs of both OpenAI and Anthropic called for global AI regulation at the UN, and the US and China are sharply divided on what that regulation should look like.

stories.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-6: Meet 'Sol' and 'Luna'
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI officially launched GPT-6, released in two versions called Sol and Luna. This is the biggest AI model release since GPT-4 and marks a significant leap in capability. In plain terms: these models are likely to be faster, smarter, and better at complex reasoning than anything publicly available before. This directly affects how useful AI tools are for everyday tasks — writing, coding, analysis — and puts massive pressure on Google and Anthropic to respond.

stories.title: Google Rushing Gemini 4 Out the Door — Way Earlier Than Expected
stories.why_it_matters: A DeepMind executive confirmed Google's Gemini 4 model is coming 'much earlier' than its originally expected year-end timeframe. Leaked details suggest Gemini 4 could cost 5 times less to run than current models and will include 3D capabilities — meaning it could understand and generate 3D content, not just text and images. For GOOG investors, the race is real and Google appears to be accelerating. The question is whether it's fast enough to keep up with OpenAI's GPT-6 launch.

stories.title: OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs Call for Global AI Regulation at the UN
stories.why_it_matters: The CEOs of both OpenAI (Sam Altman) and Anthropic (Dario Amodei) took the stage at the UN to call for a coordinated global approach to AI regulation. This is notable because these companies are simultaneously releasing increasingly powerful models while calling for guardrails. Meanwhile, Anthropic and OpenAI have both launched cheaper AI models this week — making powerful AI more accessible, but also raising safety concerns about speed of deployment outpacing oversight.

stories.title: US and China Clash Over How the World Should Regulate AI
stories.why_it_matters: At the UN this week, the US and China presented sharply different visions for how AI should be governed. The US wants regulation focused on safety, transparency, and Western democratic values. China wants a model where governments have more control over AI deployment. This is not just an academic debate — the outcome shapes whether AI becomes a tool that reinforces open societies or enables authoritarian surveillance. An upcoming Trump-Xi summit is expected to be a key battleground on this issue.

sport.summary: NRL Finals Week 3 is here — the Broncos knocked out the Titans in Finals Week 2, and tomorrow night the Dolphins host the Roosters at Suncorp. Big selection news out of the Roosters camp. In AFL, Lachie Neale's tribunal saga took a wild twist, and DCE's messy exit from Manly is making headlines.

stories.title: Broncos Defeat Titans in Finals Week 2 — Dolphins Up Next
stories.why_it_matters: The Broncos have eliminated the Titans in Finals Week 2, setting up the next round of elimination action. Tomorrow night (Friday, 7:50pm) the Dolphins host the Roosters at Suncorp Stadium — that's a home ground advantage for the Dolphins and a must-win for the Roosters. With the Gold Coast connection, this one's worth watching.

stories.title: Roosters 'Fuming' Over Brutal NRL Call — Late Panthers Changes in Cleary Chaos
stories.why_it_matters: The Roosters are reportedly fuming over a refereeing or selection-related call ahead of their Friday night final against the Dolphins. There's also late drama in the Panthers camp around Nathan Cleary, with a lineup change tipped. The Panthers face the Knights on Sunday at Accor Stadium — any Cleary fitness concern would be enormous for Penrith's premiership chances.

stories.title: DCE's Messy Manly Exit: The Not-So-Hidden Secret That Stunned the NRL World
stories.why_it_matters: A deep dive into how Daly Cherry-Evans parted ways with Manly has revealed a 'not-so-hidden secret' that has apparently stunned the NRL world. The article suggests there was a significant behind-the-scenes development that accelerated DCE's departure — though full details require reading the piece. Kevvie Walters (Broncos/Kangaroos) has also made a surprising admission about the Australian halfback pecking order, with a shootout for the Kangaroos jersey seemingly emerging.

stories.title: Lachie Neale Tribunal Drama: New Footage Changes Everything
stories.why_it_matters: AFL's Lachie Neale went to the tribunal over a strike on Collingwood's Jack Ginnivan, and new video footage emerged during the hearing that appears to have significantly changed the tribunal's assessment. The AFL world erupted on social media over the vision and the tribunal's call — described by some as 'utterly shambolic' and 'inadmissible'. A major talking point heading into the AFL finals as teams fight for premiership spots.
